text: The search begins as a paperwork problem: a convent, a file, and a son taken from her decades ago. Stephen Frears gives that search ninety-eight minutes, which means whole years get skipped and a face has to carry them. The film keeps its manners. Its subject stays polite to people she has every reason to shout at, and that politeness — practised, hard-won, faintly maddening — is where the drama actually sits, rather than in any revelation. There is comedy in it, and the comedy is what keeps her from being only a victim. The word forced does the quiet damage: she was made to live in that convent, and the institution that housed her is the one that passed the child on. It sits on the Guardian's hundred for this century among much larger productions, and earns the place by staying small — an old wrong pursued in waiting rooms, over tea, with the wrong documents.

The bar is called Strudsen — the ostrich — and nobody inside needs the joke explained. The manager wants a place of his own and will not say so aloud. The butcher would sing opera. The window cleaner, who insists on being called a polisher, loves the woman behind the bar and has arranged things so that she will never find out. Benny Andersen, a poet, wrote them, and the writing refuses the easy cruelty: these are not men crushed from outside but men not quite dissatisfied enough to move. Ninety-three minutes, most of it talk, with the pianist absorbing every confession as though listening were part of the wage. Cahiers du Cinéma's list of the hundred most beautiful films in the world found room for this small Danish room, which is the kind of choice that makes a list worth arguing with.

Eight men wait in a New York apartment for a delivery, and a two-man film crew waits with them. Shirley Clarke shot this in 1962, when a fiction dressed as a documentary was still a novelty rather than a habit, and she uses the disguise for something sharper than a gag: everyone in the room knows the camera is running, and everyone adjusts. Some perform. Some bait the crew. The drug stays mostly offscreen, the jokes run long, and the tedium is the subject rather than a lapse — a hundred and three minutes of men filling time with talk they have had before. The two behind the camera do not stay outside it, and the moment they stop being observers the film turns into an argument about who is entitled to look at whom.

A clergyman pursues a general's wife through his own head, and the film never leaves that head. Germaine Dulac gives the obsession forty-one minutes and no explanation: chases that reset, doubled figures, spaces that behave the way rooms behave in a dream, all of it serving a man in an argument with his own body. The office he holds does not protect him; if anything it supplies the charge. What makes it hold is the coldness of the handling — desire filmed as a mechanism rather than a confession, with the ridiculousness left in. French cinema in 1928 had a developed vocabulary for interior states, and this pushes that vocabulary toward the erotic and the ecclesiastical at once, then declines to apologise for either.

Tony turns down the job; five years inside have left him wanting nothing, least of all a smash-and-grab. Then he learns that Mado, who was his, belongs now to a gangster called Pierre Grutter, and the small job he refused becomes a full jewel robbery that he designs himself. That sequence of decisions is the moral architecture of the film: revenge taken up as work, then carried out with genuine professional care, and nobody involved says which motive is running the operation. Jules Dassin films Paris at the level of rented rooms, old convictions, and men who kept things warm while others were away. The robbery itself is a procedure with a schedule. What follows it fills the second half, and Dassin treats that half as the real business rather than an epilogue.

A French woman drives toward the house in northern Cameroon where she lived as a child, and the film travels with her memory instead. Most of its length is the colonial household as a girl saw it: adults idle on a veranda, visitors who arrive and stay, and the houseboy whose duties include her — the person she is closest to and the one the house ranks lowest. Claire Denis lets the child's attention set the terms, so the decisive things happen at the edge of the frame and go unexplained, because nobody explained them then. Heat, waiting, small humiliations administered with perfect courtesy. A hundred and four minutes, and the tact of it is that the woman doing the remembering does not arrange her memories to come out innocent.

Scrap metal has a price per kilo, and two boys with nothing else scheduled learn it quickly. One is wired and mouthy and never still; the other is slower, and good with horses, which in this trade counts as a qualification rather than a hobby. Their employer pays cash and decides for himself what a load is worth. Clio Barnard keeps ninety-one minutes in the present tense: the work, the money that is never much, the risks that belong entirely to the boys, and the adults who might have intervened being tired or elsewhere. The horses matter more than a summary can suggest. So does the fact that the friendship is unequal, and that both boys know which of them is being carried. The Lux Prize went to it; the film makes no case at all for its own significance.

A commune of just over two hundred people keeps a school with a single class in it: four-year-olds and twelve-year-olds at the same tables. Nicolas Philibert filmed one year of it at Saint-Étienne-sur-Usson, in the Puy-de-Dôme, with Georges Lopez teaching all of them at once. The method is plain to the point of severity. Nothing is staged, nothing is worked up into drama, and lessons, quarrels and the slow labour of learning to write are given the same weight, which is considerable. Lopez asks a question and then waits, and the waiting is where the film's respect lives; he does not raise his voice and he does not hurry, and both turn out to be decisions rather than temperament. A hundred and four minutes in one room, and the only thing in doubt is whether a child can be taught something today.

Bad City is an Iranian nowhere with rules, and one of the people keeping to them after dark is a vampire. The townspeople do not know this, and Ana Lily Amirpour is in no rush to correct them: the pressure comes from tempo rather than shocks, from streets that stay empty long after a conventional film would have filled them, and from encounters allowed to run past the point of comfort. Romance is listed second among the genres and belongs there. The film is seriously interested in whether a monster can be courted, and in what courtship would demand of both parties. Criticism has read the girl as a female monster whose violence liberates rather than punishes, and a hundred and one minutes of her walking her own town at night leaves ample room for that reading.

The tide puts a woman on a beach as though it had finished with her. What follows is movement rather than plot: she climbs, she crawls, she keeps arriving in places the cut has fastened to the sand, and some of the people she meets are other versions of herself. Maya Deren made it in 1944, when American film meant studios, contracts and schedules, and the scale here is a beach, a few interiors, and an editing logic in which distance is optional. The joins are the work. Because the journey is a search for identity, the doubling is not ornament — each duplicate argues that the self on screen is not one thing, and the argument is made in cuts rather than in explanation. Fifteen minutes, and it settles nothing on a second pass either.

The friendship starts as a practical favour: one woman helping another end a pregnancy she cannot afford. Then they lose track of each other for ten years. Agnès Varda gives the reunion no fanfare and no symmetry — Pomme sings, in a register of her own devising, Suzanne works in a community, and the film declines to rank the two lives. Songs interrupt the drama rather than decorate it; they are arguments the film would rather have in the first person. That is one way to describe the decade it came out of, when the French women's movement Varda belonged to was arguing about everything at once. Two hours, ten years, jobs and letters and children. The warmth is deliberate and slightly deceptive: almost every gentle scene rests on a legal or financial fact that could have gone the other way.

A palace has two architectures — the rooms where orders are given, and the rooms where they are carried out. Moufida Tlatli films the second kind. A prince has died, and a woman comes back to the house where she was born into service, so the film moves between what she can see now and what she was permitted to see as a girl. Servants' knowledge is the material: what is overheard, what is understood without being stated, what gets carried up a staircase along with the tray. Silence here is a working condition, kept by women who know exactly what speech costs and who develop other channels. The prince's death is the pretext; the house is the subject. Two hours, almost all of it indoors, with frosted glass and heavy curtains doing what a lock would do too crudely.

The autobiography is built rather than remembered: excerpts from her own films on one side, scenes staged for this one on the other, and Agnès Varda between them deciding which to trust. She is both subject and editor, which lets her be selective in plain sight, and selecting in plain sight turns out to be a kind of candour. Friendships take up more room than achievements. Her marriage to Jacques Demy is here, treated as a private matter conducted where everyone can see it. Beaches recur, and she lets the recurrence stay a habit of memory rather than a key to anything. The César for documentary came to it, though what lasts is smaller than a prize: a woman with decades of her own footage refusing to treat any of it as settled.
